title: If you have N instances, how do you distribute requests equally (load balancer algorithms, health checks, Kubernetes Service)?
shortTitle: If you have N instances, how do you distribute requests equally
keyPoints: A load balancer sits in front of N identical instances and picks one for each request using a configured algorithm.
Round-robin rotates through instances in order: fair for uniform requests but ignores how busy each instance is.
Least-connections sends to the instance with the fewest active requests: the better default for variable workloads.
Consistent hashing routes by a key so the same account always hits the same instance, helping local caching.
Health checks remove dead instances from the rotation so traffic is never sent to an unhealthy pod.
In Kubernetes, a Service plus kube-proxy provides round-robin-style balancing automatically behind a stable address.
For HTTP/2 or long-lived connections, use a layer-seven balancer or service mesh for true request-level balancing.

s1_definition.oneliner: A load balancer spreads requests across N healthy instances using an algorithm like round-robin or least-connections, health checks keep dead instances out of the rotation, and a Kubernetes Service does all of this automatically behind a stable address.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Load balancer** – sits in front of N identical instances and selects one for each request using a configured algorithm.
- **Round-robin** – rotates through instances in order; fair for uniform requests but ignores actual instance load.
- **Least-connections** – sends to the instance with the fewest active requests; adapts to variable request costs.
- **Consistent hashing** – routes by a key so the same client or account sticks to the same instance, helping caches.
- **Health checks** – periodically probe each instance and remove unhealthy ones from the rotation.
- **Kubernetes Service** – provides a stable virtual IP and DNS name, tracking healthy Pod endpoints via readiness probes.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India has several identical counters open and a crowd of customers arriving. The receptionist at the door decides who goes to which counter. The simplest fair rule is rotation: one each in turn (round-robin). A smarter rule is to look at which counter has the shortest queue (least-connections). For customers needing ongoing paperwork, the same customer always goes to the same clerk (consistent hashing). The receptionist only directs people to counters that are actually open (health checks), never to a closed one.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Distributing requests equally across N instances is the job of a load balancer, and the key is choosing the algorithm that matches your request-cost profile. Round-robin cycles through instances in order and is perfectly fair for uniform requests. Least-connections sends each request to the instance with the fewest active requests, adapting naturally to variable costs. Consistent hashing maps a key to an instance on a ring so the same account always hits the same instance, which helps local caching.

Health checks are what make all of this safe. The load balancer periodically probes each instance and removes any that fail from the rotation. In Kubernetes, a Service gives a stable virtual IP and DNS name and tracks healthy Pod endpoints through readiness probes, giving round-robin-style balancing with no application code.

The nuance I always mention is that kube-proxy balances TCP connections, not individual HTTP requests. For long-lived or HTTP/2 connections, you need a layer-seven ingress controller or a service mesh to truly balance request load.

Remember one sentence: put a load balancer in front of N stateless instances, gate the rotation with health checks, and pick the algorithm to fit your workload: round-robin for uniform requests, least-connections for variable ones, and consistent hashing when affinity matters.
